result.summary: Vertumnus tells Pomona how Anaxarete's cruelty drove Iphis to hang himself and turned her to stone, then reveals his true form and wins her. The narrative then turns to early Rome: the Sabine war, Juno opening the gate and Venus' Naiads blocking it, and the deification of Romulus as Quirinus and Hersilia as Ora.

scenes.title: Argument of the Fables
scenes.summary: A prose heading summarizes the tale of Anaxarete and the early history of Rome up to the deification of Romulus and Hersilia.

scenes.title: Iphis and Anaxarete
scenes.summary: Iphis, scorned by the proud Anaxarete, hangs himself at her door. Watching his funeral, she is turned to stone.
scenes.stakes: Iphis stands to lose his life through hopeless love; Anaxarete risks divine punishment for her cruelty.

scenes.title: Vertumnus Wins Pomona
scenes.summary: Vertumnus urges Pomona to yield, drops his disguise and appears radiant. She is won over.
scenes.stakes: Vertumnus risks losing Pomona; Pomona risks rejecting love.

scenes.title: The Sabine War
scenes.summary: Tarpeia betrays the citadel, the Sabines enter, Juno opens a gate and Venus has the Naiads flood it with hot water. The war ends in peace.
scenes.stakes: Rome risks being overrun in its infancy by the Sabines.

scenes.title: Romulus Taken to Heaven
scenes.summary: Mavors asks Jove to fulfil his promise. Jove sends thunder and Mavors carries Romulus off to become Quirinus.
scenes.stakes: Romulus's mortal life; the fulfilment of Jove's promise.

scenes.title: Hersilia Becomes Ora
scenes.summary: Juno sends Iris to console Hersilia, who is taken to the hill of Quirinus and raised to the sky as the goddess Ora.
scenes.stakes: Hersilia grieves for her husband and longs to see him again.

notable_quotes.reason: Iphis's dying prayer to be remembered by fame.
Links the myth to a real statue and temple at Salamis.

analysis.text: Anaxarete's hardness literally becomes stone, a punishment fitting her cruelty, and it warns Pomona against disdain.
The Roman half blends myth and Augustan-era origins, explaining the deification of Romulus as Quirinus and the cult of Ora.

legacy.text: The Tarpeian betrayal and Romulus's apotheosis became standard material in later Roman and Renaissance retellings of Rome's founding.

fun_facts.text: The Tarpeian Rock in Rome was later used as a place of execution, linked to Tarpeia's name.

language_notes.text: Teucer was an ancestor figure of Troy's royal line (the Trojan Teucer), so Anaxarete's descent is presented as ancient and noble.
'Obdurate bolt' means the stubborn door-bolt, with 'obdurate' meaning hardened and unyielding; the lover's complaint at a closed door is a conventional scene.
The Kids are stars in Auriga whose setting brings autumn storms, so the sea is at its roughest. Norican iron came from Noricum, a Roman province in the Alps.
Pæan is a title of Apollo, invoked in triumphal and victory songs; the laurel crown was the victor's wreath. Iphis bitterly gives her a conqueror's honours.
The 'twofold light' means his life and the sight of her, both of which he loses at once.
Vertumnus ends the tale of Iphis, who turned to stone; Salamis is a city in Cyprus where the statue and the temple of Venus Prospiciens were said to stand.
Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy. Numitor was the grandfather of Romulus and Remus, restored to his throne by them after Amulius had usurped it.
Tarpeia opened the citadel to the Sabines for what they wore on their left arms; they crushed her under their shields, so her death is the "just retribution".
"The son of Ilia" means Romulus; Ilia (Rhea Silvia) was his mother. Cures was a Sabine town.
A god could not undo what another god had done, so Venus could not close the gate that Juno opened.
Mavors is an old poetic name for Mars, god of war and, in Roman tradition, father of Romulus.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, perhaps meaning 'the marching one'.
Quirites is the Roman term for citizens, here the people of Romulus.
Son of Ilia: Romulus. Ilia (Rhea Silvia) was the priestess who bore him and Remus to Mars.
Latian means of Latium, the region around Rome; the Sabines were the neighbouring people Romulus's Romans merged with.
The virgin daughter of Thaumas is Iris, goddess of the rainbow and messenger of the gods.
Ora is Hersilia's divine name; 'Quirmus' is a misprint for Quirinus, the deified Romulus.

context_notes.text: Vertumnus, a god of the seasons, tells this tale in disguise to the nymph Pomona to persuade her not to reject him as Anaxarete rejected Iphis.
Quirinus was the name of the deified Romulus; Hersilia, his wife, became the goddess Ora.
Hanging garlands on a beloved's door and lying at the threshold were the traditional acts of a shut-out lover in Roman love poetry.
Vertumnus is a god of changing seasons who can take any shape. He has courted Pomona, goddess of orchards, disguised as an old woman.
Pales was a pastoral deity. Her festival, the Parilia on 21 April, was the traditional date of Rome's founding.
The temple of Janus, with gates open in war and closed in peace, stood by the Roman Forum. Naiads are nymphs of springs and streams.
Tatius was the Sabine king who ruled jointly with Romulus after the war over the abducted Sabine women.
Thunder and lightning as signs of Jove's assent are typical of Roman omens.
Hersilia was Romulus's wife, a Sabine woman. Juno, queen of the gods, pities her grief.

literary_notes.text: Anaxarete is compared to the deaf sea, hard iron and rooted rock, building a piling-up of images of her unfeeling nature.
Calling her a 'woman of iron' makes her hardness of heart literal, and so foreshadows her transformation to stone.
Iphis points bitterly to the garlands that once pleaded for love, now serving as the noose and his final reproach.
The stone already in her breast makes the metamorphosis a literal fulfilment of her character, with punishment matching her cruelty.
Vertumnus's true form is compared to the sun breaking through clouds, conveying sudden radiance after the disguise is removed.
Vertumnus plans force, but his true beauty wins her willingly, reversing the expected violence of the myth.
The Sabines are compared to silent wolves, suggesting stealth and predatory menace as they attack sleeping men.
The narrator addresses the waters directly, stressing the marvel that formerly icy springs now rival fire in heat.
Gradivus and 'the woody Palatium' use descriptive naming to give the divine descent an epic dignity.
The vanishing mortal body is compared to a lead sling-bullet that melts in flight, an image of rapid, complete dissolution.
Hersilia swears that seeing her husband will be like seeing Heaven, and she then literally ascends to heaven.
